title: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa
source: Caesar, Dē Bellō Gallicō 1.1 (c. 50 BC, trimmed)
about: Caesar opens his memoir of the Gallic War with a quick tour of the land and its peoples, the most famous first line in Latin prose.

badge.name: Three Parts
badge.about: Read the opening of Caesar's Gallic War

lines.t: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in partēs trēs,
lines.en: Gaul as a whole is divided into three parts,

q.prompt: Into how many parts is Gaul divided?

lines.t: quārum ūnam incolunt Belgae,
lines.en: one of which the Belgae inhabit,

lines.t: aliam Aquītānī,
lines.en: another the Aquitani,

lines.t: tertiam quī ipsōrum linguā Celtae, nostrā Gallī appellantur.
lines.en: and the third those who in their own language are called Celts, in ours Gauls.

q.prompt: What do the Romans call the people who call themselves Celts?

lines.t: Hī omnēs linguā, īnstitūtīs, lēgibus inter sē differunt.
lines.en: All these differ from one another in language, customs and laws.

q.prompt: How do these peoples differ?

lines.t: Hōrum omnium fortissimī sunt Belgae.
lines.en: Of all these, the bravest are the Belgae.

q.prompt: Who does Caesar call the bravest?

title: Admīror, pariēs
source: Pompeii wall inscriptions: CIL IV 429, 1679, 2146, 2331, 1904 (before AD 79)
about: Vesuvius buried Pompeii in AD 79 and preserved thousands of messages on its walls. Here are five: an election poster, a bar's price list, a lonely lover, a doodled maze and a word of pity for the wall itself. Abbreviations are written out.

badge.name: Wall Scrawler
badge.about: Read five messages from the walls of Pompeii

lines.t: Gāium Iūlium Polybium aedīlem ōrō vōs faciātis.
lines.en: Elect Gaius Julius Polybius aedile, I beg you.

lines.t: Pānem bonum fert.
lines.en: He brings good bread.

q.prompt: What does the poster promise about Polybius?

lines.t: Edone dīcit: assibus hīc bibitur;
lines.en: Edone says: here you can drink for one as;

lines.t: dipundium sī dederis, meliōra bibēs;
lines.en: if you pay two, you will drink better;

lines.t: quattus sī dederis, vīna Falerna bibēs.
lines.en: if you pay four, you will drink Falernian.

q.prompt: How much does the best wine cost at Edone's bar?

lines.t: Vibius Restitūtus hīc sōlus dormīvit et Urbānam suam dēsīderābat.
lines.en: Vibius Restitutus slept here alone and missed his Urbana.

q.prompt: Why was Vibius unhappy?

lines.t: Labyrinthus. Hīc habitat Mīnōtaurus.
lines.en: The Labyrinth. Here lives the Minotaur.

lines.t: Admīror, pariēs, tē nōn cecidisse ruīnīs,
lines.en: I am amazed, wall, that you have not collapsed in ruins,

lines.t: quī tot scrīptōrum taedia sustineās.
lines.en: you who hold up the tiresome scribbles of so many writers.

q.prompt: Why is the writer amazed that the wall still stands?

title: Ōdī et amō
source: Catullus 85 (c. 55 BC) and Martial, Epigrams 1.32 (c. AD 85)
about: Two famous Roman epigrams about feelings that refuse to explain themselves: Catullus torn between love and hate, and Martial disliking a man for no reason he can name.

lines.t: Ōdī et amō.
lines.en: I hate and I love.

q.prompt: What does Catullus feel?

lines.t: Quārē id faciam, fortasse requīris.
lines.en: Why I do that, perhaps you ask.

lines.t: Nesciō, sed fierī sentiō et excrucior.
lines.en: I don't know, but I feel it happening, and I am in torment.

q.prompt: Can Catullus explain his feelings?

lines.t: Nōn amō tē, Sabidī, nec possum dīcere quārē:
lines.en: I don't like you, Sabidius, and I can't say why:

q.prompt: Why does Martial dislike Sabidius?

lines.t: hoc tantum possum dīcere, nōn amō tē.
lines.en: all I can say is this: I don't like you.

title: Annōs ūndēvīgintī nātus
source: Augustus, Rēs Gestae Dīvī Augustī 1–3 (AD 14, trimmed)
about: Rome's first emperor wrote his own record of his deeds and had it set up on bronze pillars outside his tomb. The best copy survives on a temple wall in Ankara. It opens with a nineteen-year-old raising an army and avenging his adoptive father, Julius Caesar.

badge.name: Princeps
badge.about: Read the opening of Augustus' Res Gestae

lines.t: Annōs ūndēvīgintī nātus exercitum prīvātō cōnsiliō et prīvātā impēnsā comparāvī,
lines.en: At nineteen years of age I raised an army on my own initiative and at my own expense,

q.prompt: How old was Augustus when he raised his army?

lines.t: per quem rem pūblicam ā dominātiōne factiōnis oppressam in lībertātem vindicāvī.
lines.en: and with it I set the Republic free from the tyranny of a faction that was crushing it.

lines.t: Quī parentem meum trucīdāvērunt, eōs in exilium expulī
lines.en: Those who butchered my father I drove into exile,

q.prompt: What did Augustus do to his father's killers?

lines.t: iūdiciīs lēgitimīs ultus eōrum facinus,
lines.en: avenging their crime through lawful courts,

lines.t: et posteā bellum īnferentīs reī pūblicae vīcī bis aciē.
lines.en: and later, when they made war on the Republic, I defeated them twice in battle.

q.prompt: How many times did he beat them in battle?

lines.t: Bella terrā et marī cīvīlia externaque tōtō in orbe terrārum saepe gessī,
lines.en: I often waged wars, civil and foreign, on land and sea, all over the world,

lines.t: victorque omnibus veniam petentibus cīvibus pepercī.
lines.en: and as victor I spared all citizens who asked for mercy.

q.prompt: How did he treat citizens who asked for mercy?

lines.t: Externās gentēs, quibus tūtō ignōscī potuit, cōnservāre quam excīdere māluī.
lines.en: Foreign peoples who could safely be pardoned I preferred to spare rather than wipe out.

lines.t: Nāvēs cēpī sescentās praeter eās, sī quae minōrēs quam trirēmēs fuērunt.
lines.en: I captured six hundred ships, not counting any smaller than triremes.

q.prompt: How many ships did Augustus capture?

title: Īcare, ubi es?
about: The inventor Daedalus is trapped on Crete by King Minos. He builds wings of feathers and wax for himself and his son Icarus, and warns the boy to fly between the sea and the sun.

badge.name: Wax Wings
badge.about: Read Ovid's story of Daedalus and Icarus

lines.t: Terrās licet, inquit, et undās obstruat:
lines.en: He may block the land and the sea, he said,

lines.t: et caelum certē patet; ībimus illāc:
lines.en: but the sky at least lies open; that is the way we will go.

q.prompt: How does Daedalus plan to escape?

lines.t: omnia possideat, nōn possidet āera Mīnōs.
lines.en: Minos may own everything, but he does not own the air.

lines.t: Inter utrumque volā.
lines.en: Fly between the two.

q.prompt: Daedalus tells Icarus to fly between which two dangers?

lines.t: cum puer audācī coepit gaudēre volātū
lines.en: when the boy began to delight in his daring flight

lines.t: dēseruitque ducem caelīque cupīdine tractus altius ēgit iter.
lines.en: and left his guide, and, drawn by longing for the sky, flew higher.

q.prompt: Why did Icarus fly higher?

lines.t: rapidī vīcīnia sōlis mollit odōrātās, pennārum vincula, cērās;
lines.en: The nearness of the scorching sun softens the fragrant wax that bound the feathers;

lines.t: tābuerant cērae: nūdōs quatit ille lacertōs,
lines.en: the wax had melted: he flaps his bare arms,

q.prompt: What happened to the wax?

lines.t: at pater īnfēlīx, nec iam pater, Īcare, dīxit,
lines.en: But the unhappy father, a father no longer, cried, 'Icarus!'

q.prompt: Why is Daedalus 'a father no longer'?
options: Icarus has fallen to his death

lines.t: Īcare, dīxit, ubi es? quā tē regiōne requīram?
lines.en: 'Icarus,' he cried, 'where are you? Where in the world shall I look for you?'

title: Fortēs fortūna iuvat
source: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 6.16.4–20 (c. AD 106, trimmed)
about: The historian Tacitus asked Pliny how his uncle, Pliny the Elder, died. The uncle commanded the Roman fleet at Misenum when Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, and he sailed toward the mountain to rescue people on the shore.

badge.name: Eyewitness
badge.about: Read Pliny's letter on the eruption of Vesuvius

lines.t: Erat Mīsēnī classemque imperiō praesēns regēbat.
lines.en: He was at Misenum, commanding the fleet in person.

q.prompt: What was the elder Pliny doing at Misenum?

lines.t: Nōnum Kal. Septembrēs hōrā ferē septimā māter mea indicat eī
lines.en: On 24 August, at about the seventh hour, my mother points out to him

lines.t: appārēre nūbem inūsitātā et magnitūdine et speciē.
lines.en: a cloud of unusual size and shape.

q.prompt: What did Pliny's mother notice?

lines.t: Properat illūc unde aliī fugiunt,
lines.en: He hurries to the place that everyone else is fleeing,

lines.t: Iam nāvibus cinis incidēbat, quō propius accēderent, calidior et dēnsior;
lines.en: Ash was already falling on the ships, hotter and thicker the closer they came;

lines.t: Fortēs, inquit, fortūna iuvat: Pompōniānum pete.
lines.en: Fortune helps the brave, he said: make for Pomponianus.

q.prompt: What does he say when the helmsman wants to turn back?

lines.t: Iam diēs alibī, illīc nox omnibus noctibus nigrior dēnsiorque;
lines.en: By now it was day elsewhere; there it was night, blacker and thicker than any night;

q.prompt: What was strange about the next morning?
options: it stayed as dark as night

lines.t: Innītēns servolīs duōbus assurrēxit et statim concidit,
lines.en: Leaning on two slaves he stood up, and at once collapsed,

lines.t: corpus inventum integrum illaesum opertumque ut fuerat indūtus:
lines.en: his body was found whole and unharmed, clothed just as he had been:

q.prompt: How was his body found?

lines.t: habitus corporis quiēscentī quam dēfūnctō similior.
lines.en: he looked more like a man asleep than a dead one.
